name: Pozole Rojo with Pork & Guajillo Chile
why: Mexico’s most beloved winter soup — hominy plump in a deep guajillo-chile broth, slow-simmered pork, and a pile of sharp garnishes. The ultimate crowd-pleaser: it makes 10+ bowls, freezes beautifully, and tastes even better the next day.
author: Henry
ingredients: 1.5 lbs guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded (or 2 bags)
1 lb bone-in pork (shoulder or backbone — espinazo is the traditional cut)
4 tsp salt, plus more to taste
2 tins (75 oz total) white hominy, drained
Shredded cabbage or iceberg lettuce, to serve
Limes, cut in half, to serve

steps: Boil the guajillo chiles in water until tender, about 15 minutes, then blend with a cup of the cooking water until smooth. Strain the puree through a fine-mesh sieve to catch seeds and skins.
In a large pot, combine the pork, the unpeeled head of garlic, and enough water to cover by 2 inches. Add 4 tsp salt.
Bring to a boil, skim off any scum, then reduce to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for about 1 hour, until the pork is fully cooked.
Add the drained hominy and the strained guajillo sauce to the pot.
Return to a boil, then simmer on medium heat for about 30 minutes so the hominy, pork, and chile flavours meld. Taste and salt if needed.
Ladle the pozole into bowls and pile on the garnishes: diced onion, shredded cabbage, a shake of dried oregano, and a big squeeze of fresh lime.

pro_tips: Cook the garlic in its whole unpeeled head — it keeps from dissolving into the broth and you can just squeeze the cloves out before serving. Use bone-in pork (backbone is traditional): the marrow is what gives the broth its deep, porky richness.
Pozole improves with time — leftovers taste even better the next day and it freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Serve with tostadas for extra crunch.
